questions.text: Which is the largest planet in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Jupiter's diameter is about eleven times that of Earth, making it larger than all the other planets combined.

questions.text: Which planet is called the Red Planet?
questions.explanation: Iron oxide dust on the Martian surface gives Mars its characteristic reddish colour.

questions.text: Which planet has the highest surface temperature?
questions.explanation: Venus has a dense carbon dioxide atmosphere that traps heat, giving surface temperatures near 460 degrees Celsius even though Mercury is closer to the Sun.

questions.text: Which planet is tilted almost on its side, with an axial tilt of about 98 degrees?
questions.explanation: Uranus rotates with its axis nearly in the plane of its orbit, so its poles alternately face the Sun.

questions.text: Which planet takes about 243 Earth days to complete one rotation on its axis?
questions.explanation: Venus has the slowest rotation of any planet, and it also rotates in a retrograde direction.

questions.text: Which is the largest natural satellite in the solar system?
questions.explanation: Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is larger than the planet Mercury.

questions.text: Which moon of Saturn has a dense atmosphere rich in nitrogen?
questions.explanation: Titan is the only moon known to have a thick atmosphere, composed mainly of nitrogen with some methane.

questions.text: Which body lost its status as a planet when the International Astronomical Union redefined the term in 2006?
questions.explanation: Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet because it has not cleared the neighbourhood around its orbit.

questions.text: The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of which two planets?
questions.explanation: The main asteroid belt occupies the region between Mars and Jupiter.

questions.text: Which is the largest object in the asteroid belt?
questions.explanation: Ceres contains roughly a quarter of the belt's total mass and is classified as a dwarf planet.

questions.text: The energy radiated by the Sun is produced by
questions.explanation: Hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium in the Sun's core, releasing energy according to mass-energy equivalence.

questions.text: The visible surface of the Sun is called the
questions.explanation: The photosphere is the layer from which sunlight escapes into space, at a temperature of about 5,500 degrees Celsius.

questions.text: Light from the Sun takes approximately how long to reach the Earth?
questions.explanation: At about 150 million kilometres and a light speed of 300,000 km per second, sunlight takes roughly 8 minutes 20 seconds.

questions.text: Which star is nearest to the Sun?
questions.explanation: Proxima Centauri lies about 4.24 light years away, closer than any other known star.

questions.text: A fragment of rock from space that survives its passage through the atmosphere and lands on Earth is called a
questions.explanation: A meteoroid becomes a meteor while burning in the atmosphere and is called a meteorite once it reaches the ground.

questions.text: A solar eclipse occurs when
options: the Earth's shadow falls on the Sun
the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
the Sun comes between the Earth and the Moon
the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth
questions.explanation: During a solar eclipse the Moon blocks sunlight and casts its shadow on part of the Earth's surface.

questions.text: A lunar eclipse can occur only at the phase of
questions.explanation: Only at full moon is the Earth positioned directly between the Sun and the Moon so that its shadow can fall on the Moon.

questions.text: The same face of the Moon is always turned towards the Earth because
options: the Moon does not rotate at all
the Moon orbits in the plane of the ecliptic
the Earth's gravity stops lunar rotation
the Moon's rotation period equals its period of revolution
questions.explanation: This synchronous rotation means the Moon turns once on its axis in exactly the time it takes to orbit the Earth.

questions.text: Ocean tides are caused mainly by the gravitational pull of the
questions.explanation: Although the Sun also contributes, the Moon is far closer and exerts roughly twice the tide-raising force.

questions.text: Spring tides, the highest tides of the month, occur at
questions.explanation: At new and full moon the Sun, Earth and Moon are aligned, so their tide-raising forces add together.

questions.text: Who was the first human being to travel into space?
questions.explanation: Yuri Gagarin orbited the Earth aboard Vostok 1 in April 1961.

questions.text: Who was the first person to set foot on the Moon?
questions.explanation: Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface during the Apollo 11 mission.

questions.text: The seasons on Earth are caused by
options: the changing distance of the Earth from the Sun
the rotation of the Earth on its axis
the tilt of the Earth's axis together with its revolution
questions.explanation: Because the axis stays tilted at a fixed angle as the Earth orbits, each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight for part of the year.

questions.text: The Earth's axis is inclined to the plane of its orbit at an angle of about
questions.explanation: This tilt of roughly 23.5 degrees from the vertical produces the annual cycle of seasons.

questions.text: The summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere falls on about
questions.explanation: On 21 June the Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, giving the Northern Hemisphere its longest day.

questions.text: The Tropic of Cancer lies at a latitude of
questions.explanation: The Tropic of Cancer marks the northern limit at which the Sun can be directly overhead.

questions.text: The lowest layer of the Earth's atmosphere is the
questions.explanation: The troposphere extends from the surface to about 8-16 km and contains almost all weather phenomena.

questions.text: The ozone layer is located in the
questions.explanation: Ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere at heights of roughly 15 to 35 kilometres.

questions.text: Most meteors entering the Earth's atmosphere burn up in the
questions.explanation: Friction with the increasingly dense air of the mesosphere vaporises most incoming meteoroids.

questions.text: Which region of the atmosphere reflects radio waves back to the Earth, making long-distance radio communication possible?
questions.explanation: Ionised gas layers in the ionosphere bend and reflect radio waves back towards the surface.

questions.text: Which gas is present in the largest proportion in dry air?
questions.explanation: Nitrogen makes up about 78 per cent of dry air by volume.

questions.text: Oxygen forms approximately what percentage of dry air by volume?
questions.explanation: Oxygen accounts for roughly 21 per cent of dry air, the second most abundant constituent after nitrogen.

questions.text: The boundary separating the troposphere from the stratosphere is called the
questions.explanation: The tropopause marks the level at which the fall of temperature with height in the troposphere ceases.

questions.text: Which is the third most abundant gas in dry air?
questions.explanation: Argon makes up about 0.93 per cent of dry air, more than carbon dioxide or any other trace gas.

questions.text: Atmospheric pressure is measured with a
questions.explanation: A barometer measures the weight of the column of air above it, usually in millibars or millimetres of mercury.

questions.text: In the Northern Hemisphere, winds circulating around a low-pressure centre blow
questions.explanation: The Coriolis deflection to the right in the Northern Hemisphere makes air spiral anticlockwise into a cyclone.

questions.text: The Coriolis effect, which deflects winds and ocean currents, is a consequence of
options: unequal heating of land and sea
the Earth's revolution around the Sun
questions.explanation: Because the Earth spins beneath moving air, winds appear deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern.

questions.text: Which cloud type is associated with thunderstorms and heavy showers?
questions.explanation: Cumulonimbus clouds are tall vertical clouds produced by strong convection and bring thunder, lightning and heavy rain.

questions.text: Lines joining places receiving equal amounts of rainfall are called
questions.explanation: Isohyets are used on climatic maps to show the distribution of precipitation.

questions.text: Jet streams are fast-moving air currents found in the
questions.explanation: Jet streams flow near the tropopause, at heights of roughly 9 to 12 kilometres.

questions.text: El Nino refers to the abnormal warming of surface waters in the
questions.explanation: El Nino is a periodic warming of the eastern and central equatorial Pacific that disturbs weather patterns worldwide.

questions.text: The summer monsoon rains of Pakistan and India are brought by winds blowing from the
questions.explanation: Moisture-laden south-west monsoon winds blow from the Indian Ocean towards the heated land mass in summer.

questions.text: The belt of calm, light and variable winds lying near the equator is known as the
questions.explanation: Intense heating at the equator causes air to rise rather than blow horizontally, producing a zone of calms.

questions.text: Granite is an example of which type of rock?
questions.explanation: Granite crystallises slowly from magma deep below the surface, making it a coarse-grained intrusive igneous rock.

questions.text: Marble is formed by the metamorphism of
questions.explanation: Heat and pressure recrystallise the calcite in limestone to produce marble.

questions.text: Slate is a metamorphic rock formed from
questions.explanation: Low-grade metamorphism of fine-grained shale produces slate, which splits into thin sheets.

questions.text: Which mineral occupies the top position on the Mohs scale of hardness?
questions.explanation: Diamond is rated 10 on the Mohs scale and can scratch every other mineral.

questions.text: Which element is most abundant in the Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Oxygen forms roughly 46 per cent of the crust by weight, mostly combined in silicate minerals.

questions.text: Which metal is most abundant in the Earth's crust?
questions.explanation: Aluminium makes up about 8 per cent of the crust, more than any other metal.

questions.text: Bauxite is the chief ore of
questions.explanation: Bauxite is a hydrated aluminium oxide from which almost all commercial aluminium is extracted.

questions.text: Cinnabar is the principal ore of
questions.explanation: Cinnabar is mercuric sulphide and is roasted to obtain metallic mercury.

questions.text: The Earth's core consists mainly of
questions.explanation: Seismic evidence and meteorite composition indicate a core dominated by iron with about 5-10 per cent nickel.

questions.text: Which layer accounts for the greatest share of the Earth's volume?
questions.explanation: The mantle is about 2,900 kilometres thick and makes up roughly 84 per cent of the Earth's volume.

questions.text: The boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle is known as the
questions.explanation: The Mohorovicic discontinuity, or Moho, is marked by a sudden increase in seismic wave velocity.

questions.text: The Earth's magnetic field is generated chiefly in the
questions.explanation: Convection currents of molten iron in the outer core act as a dynamo that produces the magnetic field.

questions.text: The point on the Earth's surface directly above the focus of an earthquake is the
questions.explanation: Shaking is generally strongest at the epicentre because it is nearest the source of the waves.

questions.text: Which seismic waves travel fastest and are recorded first at a seismic station?
questions.explanation: P waves are compressional waves and move faster than shear or surface waves, so they arrive first.

questions.text: Which seismic waves cannot pass through liquids, providing evidence that the outer core is molten?
questions.explanation: S waves are shear waves, and liquids cannot sustain shear stress, so they are blocked by the outer core.

questions.text: Tsunamis are most commonly generated by
questions.explanation: Sudden vertical displacement of the sea floor during a submarine earthquake sets off long-wavelength waves.

questions.text: The theory of continental drift was put forward by
questions.explanation: Wegener proposed in 1912 that the continents had once been joined and had since drifted apart.

questions.text: The name given to the single supercontinent that is believed to have existed before the continents drifted apart is
questions.explanation: Pangaea later split into Laurasia in the north and Gondwana in the south.

questions.text: The Ring of Fire, a zone of frequent earthquakes and volcanoes, surrounds the
questions.explanation: Subduction of oceanic plates around the margins of the Pacific produces this belt of volcanic and seismic activity.

questions.text: Mid-ocean ridges are formed at
questions.explanation: Where plates move apart, magma rises to fill the gap and creates new oceanic crust along a ridge.

questions.text: The Himalayas were formed by the collision of the
questions.explanation: The northward movement of the Indian plate into Eurasia crumpled the intervening sediments into fold mountains.

questions.text: The San Andreas Fault in California is an example of a
questions.explanation: At a transform boundary two plates slide horizontally past each other without creating or destroying crust.

questions.text: The hypothesis of sea-floor spreading was proposed by
questions.explanation: Harry Hess suggested in the early 1960s that new ocean floor forms at ridges and spreads outwards.

questions.text: Which is the largest and deepest ocean on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Pacific covers about a third of the Earth's surface and contains the deepest known trenches.

questions.text: The deepest known point of the world's oceans lies in the
questions.explanation: Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench of the western Pacific reaches nearly 11,000 metres below sea level.

questions.text: The average salinity of sea water is about
questions.explanation: Sea water contains roughly 35 grams of dissolved salts per kilogram, that is 35 parts per thousand.

questions.text: The most abundant salt dissolved in sea water is
questions.explanation: Sodium chloride accounts for about 77 per cent of the dissolved solids in sea water.

questions.text: Water covers approximately what fraction of the Earth's surface?
questions.explanation: Oceans and seas cover close to 71 per cent of the planet's surface area.

questions.text: The Gulf Stream is
options: a cold current of the Pacific Ocean
a cold current of the Indian Ocean
a warm current of the North Atlantic Ocean
a warm current of the Southern Ocean
questions.explanation: The Gulf Stream carries warm water north-eastwards across the Atlantic and moderates the climate of north-west Europe.

questions.text: Which gas is the largest single contributor to the human-induced greenhouse effect?
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide released by burning fossil fuels accounts for the greatest share of the added radiative forcing.

questions.text: Greenhouse gases warm the lower atmosphere chiefly by absorbing
options: infrared radiation emitted by the Earth
questions.explanation: They allow short-wave sunlight to pass through but absorb the long-wave infrared radiation given off by the warmed surface.

questions.text: Without the natural greenhouse effect, the average surface temperature of the Earth would be about
questions.explanation: Natural greenhouse warming raises the mean surface temperature from roughly minus 18 degrees Celsius to about 15 degrees Celsius.

questions.text: Paddy fields, livestock and landfills are major sources of which greenhouse gas?
questions.explanation: Methane is produced by anaerobic decomposition of organic matter in flooded soils, animal guts and waste dumps.

questions.text: The chemical formula of ozone is
questions.explanation: Ozone is a triatomic allotrope of oxygen.

questions.text: The ozone layer protects life on Earth by absorbing
questions.explanation: Stratospheric ozone absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet-B radiation before it reaches the surface.

questions.text: Depletion of the ozone layer is caused mainly by
questions.explanation: Chlorine atoms released from CFCs by ultraviolet light catalyse the destruction of ozone molecules.

questions.text: The most severe seasonal thinning of the ozone layer is observed over
questions.explanation: Extremely cold polar stratospheric clouds over Antarctica speed up the chlorine reactions that destroy ozone each spring.

questions.text: The Montreal Protocol of 1987 deals with
options: substances that deplete the ozone layer
questions.explanation: It obliged countries to phase out the production and use of CFCs, halons and other ozone-depleting chemicals.

questions.text: The Kyoto Protocol, which set binding limits on greenhouse gas emissions, was adopted in
questions.explanation: It was agreed at the third Conference of the Parties in Kyoto in December 1997 and came into force in 2005.

questions.text: The Paris Agreement on climate change was adopted in
questions.explanation: It was concluded at COP21 in Paris in December 2015 and entered into force the following year.

questions.text: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change was opened for signature at the Earth Summit held in
questions.explanation: The 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro produced the UNFCCC along with the Convention on Biological Diversity.

questions.text: The first United Nations Conference on the Human Environment was held in Stockholm in
questions.explanation: The 1972 Stockholm Conference led to the creation of the United Nations Environment Programme.

questions.text: The Ramsar Convention is concerned with the conservation of
questions.explanation: Signed in Ramsar, Iran, in 1971, it provides for the protection of wetlands of international importance.

questions.text: CITES is an international agreement that regulates
questions.explanation: The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species controls cross-border trade in threatened plants and animals.

questions.text: The Basel Convention regulates the
questions.explanation: It was adopted in 1989 to control the export of hazardous waste, particularly from developed to developing countries.

questions.text: IPCC stands for
questions.explanation: The IPCC was established by the World Meteorological Organization and UNEP to assess the science of climate change.

questions.text: World Environment Day is observed every year on
questions.explanation: The United Nations designated 5 June, the opening day of the 1972 Stockholm Conference, as World Environment Day.

questions.text: The International Day for the Preservation of the Ozone Layer is observed on
questions.explanation: It marks 16 September 1987, the day the Montreal Protocol was signed.

questions.text: Acid rain is caused mainly by atmospheric emissions of
options: sulphur dioxide and oxides of nitrogen
questions.explanation: These gases dissolve in cloud droplets to form sulphuric and nitric acids that fall with the rain.

questions.text: Rain is generally described as acid rain when its pH falls below about
questions.explanation: Unpolluted rain is already slightly acidic at pH 5.6 because of dissolved carbon dioxide, so lower values indicate pollution.

questions.text: Which pollutant from vehicle exhaust combines with haemoglobin and reduces the blood's capacity to carry oxygen?
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen, forming carboxyhaemoglobin.

questions.text: Photochemical smog is produced by the action of sunlight on
questions.explanation: Sunlight drives reactions between nitrogen oxides and unburnt hydrocarbons to form ground-level ozone and other irritants.

questions.text: PM2.5 in air-quality reports refers to particulate matter with a diameter smaller than
questions.explanation: These fine particles are small enough to penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream.

questions.text: Eutrophication of lakes and rivers is caused by an excess of
questions.explanation: Nutrient runoff from fertilizers triggers algal blooms whose decay depletes dissolved oxygen in the water.

questions.text: Biochemical oxygen demand is used as a measure of
questions.explanation: BOD records the oxygen consumed by micro-organisms in breaking down organic matter, so a high value indicates heavy pollution.

questions.text: Minamata disease resulted from poisoning by
questions.explanation: Industrial discharge of methylmercury into Minamata Bay in Japan contaminated fish eaten by local people.

questions.text: Itai-itai disease, marked by severe bone pain, was caused by poisoning with
questions.explanation: Cadmium from mine waste entered rice fields in Japan and accumulated in the bones of those who ate the rice.

questions.text: Blue baby syndrome in infants is associated with drinking water containing excess
questions.explanation: Nitrate is converted to nitrite in the body and interferes with the oxygen-carrying ability of haemoglobin.

questions.text: Excess fluoride in drinking water causes
questions.explanation: Fluorosis mottles the teeth and, in severe cases, deforms the bones and joints.

questions.text: The intensity of noise is measured in
questions.explanation: The decibel is a logarithmic unit expressing sound level relative to a standard reference intensity.

questions.text: Which of the following is a non-renewable source of energy?
questions.explanation: Coal is a fossil fuel formed over millions of years and cannot be replaced on a human time scale.

questions.text: A photovoltaic cell converts
questions.explanation: Semiconductor materials in a solar cell release electrons when struck by photons, producing an electric current.

questions.text: Geothermal energy is obtained from
questions.explanation: Hot rocks and underground water heated by the Earth's internal heat are tapped to raise steam for turbines.

questions.text: The main combustible constituent of biogas is
questions.explanation: Biogas from anaerobic digestion is roughly 50 to 70 per cent methane, the rest being mainly carbon dioxide.

questions.text: A wind turbine generates electricity from the
questions.explanation: Moving air turns the blades, and the rotating shaft drives a generator that produces electricity.

questions.text: Volcanic activity is most closely associated with which type of plate boundary in addition to divergent boundaries?
questions.explanation: At convergent boundaries an oceanic plate is subducted, melts at depth and feeds volcanoes above the subduction zone.

questions.text: The rigid outer shell of the Earth, made up of the crust and the uppermost mantle, is called the
questions.explanation: The lithosphere is broken into the tectonic plates that move over the weaker asthenosphere below.
